list.listitem: In trigger finger, there is a characteristic thickening of the synovium of the flexor tendon system due to inflammation, characterized by a palpable, painful nodule.

Primary disease is most commonly seen in middle aged women from degenerative changes in the flexor tendons. Studies historically have failed to demonstrate inflammation. Secondary disease is characterized by changes that affect connective tissue such as in diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, and gout.
Trigger finger is among the most common reasons for referral to hand specialist.
Initial treatment of choice for subjective or objective triggering of finger, usually accompanied by tenderness at the A1 pulley, is a cortiosteroid injection.
A small RCT of 50 patients in the primary care setting found good evidence for efficacy of steroid injection for trigger finger. A systematic review identified two other studies with similar results.

Injection is indicated if unresponsive to a prior trial of NSAIDs and/or splinting, for recurrence of triggering after one previously successful injection (can do second injection), or when there is a desire to avoid surgical intervention (patient choice, poor surgical candidate).

Consider referral to an orthopedic surgeon or hand surgeron for injection if you are uncomfortable doing the procedure, if a pediatric patient, after 2 failed injections in a patient, and after 1 failed injection in a diabetic patient.

Consider referral for surgical trigger finger release if: (1) lack of success after initial injection, particularly in diabetics; (2) recurrence of triggering after 1 successful cortisone injection; (3) after 2 cortisone injections given 3 months apart or (4) prior history of unresponsiveness to a prior cortisone injection for trigger finger in another digit.
Steroid injection may be placed into the flexor tendon sheath or subcutaneously around the A1 pulley (portion of flexor tendon sheath over the palmar surface of MCP joints).
Injection into subcutaneous tissues around the A1 pulley is easier and gave better clinical outcomes than injection into the tendon sheath alone.

A small RCT found better pain relief with needle-free jet lidocaine administration prior to injection. Another small RCT with 64 patients found more pain with betamethasone than methylprednisolone, but the difference was not statistically significant.

Inject using 27 gauge needle a mixture of 1.0 mL (6.0 mg) of betamethasone sodium phosphate/acetate solution (Celestone Soluspan) and 0.5 mL (5 mg) of 1% lidocaine. Can also use triamcinolone 0.5 ml of 10 mg/ml with 0.5 ml or 1% lidocaine. Increasing the pH by using buffered lidocaine may reduce injection site pain.

Identify the point on the palm where the A1 pulley can be safely injected (see ). It is important to understand the different anatomical relationship of the neurovascular bundles in index and ring fingers since they cross in close proximity to the A1 pulley. For index finger A1 pulley, inject at palmar crease in a line drawn from medial aspect of pisiform bone directly to index finger; for little finger, inject at palmar crease at line drawn from medial aspect of navicular tubercle bone directly to the little finger. Novice physcians often inject at the base of the digit - above the A1 pulley, increasing the risk of treatment failure.

The longitudinal axis of the neurovascular bundles follows the midline of the middle and ring fingers. For middle and ring fingers, the A1 pulley site of injection is at the palmar crease in the midline of each digit. There is less concern about injecting at the digital nerve.

Trigger thumb is injected by introducing the needle at 45 degrees to the skin in the line of the longitudinal central markings on the thumb (see ). Do not point the needle toward the ulnar or radial side of the thumb. Inject where the longitudinal markings cross the proximal crease of the thumb. Use a 23 gauge needle with 1 ml of steroid and 1 ml of local anesthetic.
Identify the injection site (above and and ) and mark with a pen.
Betadine prep, then spray ethyl chloride on site for local anesthesia.
Carefully inject subcutaneously; assess impact on triggering post-injection.
Apply bandaid or simple dressing; reinforce signs and symptoms of infection.
Routine splinting is not recommended.
Advise the patient to limit strenous use of the injected digit for 1-2 days.
Self-limiting pain at injection site.
Inflammatory reaction to injection; recommend watchful waiting and possibly NSAIDs.
Dermal or subcutaneous atrophy, hypopigmentation of skin due to corticosteroids.
Infection of flexor sheath (rare): refer to hand surgeon for incision and drainage and IV antibiotics.
Digital nerve injection: refer to hand surgery.
Tendon rupture (one reported in literature): refer to hand surgeon.
Erratic blood glucose levels in diabetic patients for up to a week have been reported.
Note that a patient watching a "painful procedure" increases their perception of pain and unpleasantness.
Vasovagal syncope
Signs or symptoms of infection warrant immediate evaluation.
Two weeks to assess response to treatment; earlier if patient has increase in pain, redness or triggering that might be consistent with a infection of the flexor sheath.

Additional injection of cortisone may be done at 3 month intervals for a maximum of 3 injections per finger; failure of prior injection therapy for trigger fingers in same patient may warrant early referral for hand surgery evaluation.

4 to 6 weeks of splinting of affected finger if manual laborer.
